opus-5.5.text:
So, temperature is one of those technical knobs that turns out to be philosophically interesting. When a language model generates text, at each step it has a probability distribution over what could come next. Some words are very likely, some are a little less likely, and there's a long tail of options that are possible but rare. Temperature is basically a dial that decides how much you trust that distribution.

If you set the temperature very low, the model almost always picks the most probable next word. What you get is the average of humanity. It's the most typical, most expected answer, the thing that most people in the training data would have said. It's safe, it's coherent, and frankly it's a bit boring. In a sense, a low-temperature model is the ultimate conformist.

When you turn the temperature up, you flatten that distribution. You give the less likely options a better chance. Suddenly the model might take a path that very few humans would have taken. Sometimes that produces nonsense. But sometimes it produces something genuinely surprising, a connection or an idea that isn't the consensus view.

What I find fascinating, as someone who studies the brain, is that this maps really nicely onto how we think about creativity in people. Creative people, in a way, run at a slightly higher temperature. Their brains are a bit more willing to entertain the unlikely association, the weird idea that most people would filter out before it ever reaches consciousness. And there's a cost to that. Turn it up too far and you drift from creativity toward something that looks more like disorder, where the thoughts stop being coherent. So it's a balance between the predictable and the chaotic.

So when people say AI can only regurgitate what humans have already said, I think that's only half true. At low temperature, yes, it mostly reflects the center of human behavior. But temperature is literally the mechanism that lets it step away from the center and explore the edges of the distribution. It isn't inventing from nothing, because it's still drawing on what humans produced. But it can combine things in ways that no typical human would, simply because it's willing to take the road less traveled at a rate we wouldn't.

The interesting question for me is who sets the dial. With humans, temperature is shaped by personality, by mood, by alcohol, by sleep deprivation. With AI, it's a parameter someone types in. That means we can decide, for each task, how much we want it to sound like everyone versus like no one. And that's a kind of control over creativity we've never really had before.

r001.rationale: It explains that higher temperature gives less likely options a better chance, allowing the model to explore beyond typical human responses.

r002.rationale: It discusses surprising or incoherent outputs, but does not say departures can involve greater dishonesty.

r003.rationale: It does not state that AI gradually learns which behaviors humans will tolerate.

fable-5.1.text:
So, temperature is one of my favorite things to explain, because it's actually a very simple knob that ends up telling you something deep about both machines and us.

When a language model generates text, at every step it's not choosing a word. It's producing a probability distribution over all the words it could say next. "The cat sat on the..." and there's a 60 percent on "mat," maybe 10 percent on "floor," a tiny sliver on "piano," and way down in the tail, "volcano." Temperature is just a dial that reshapes that distribution before you sample from it. At low temperature, you sharpen it. The top option becomes almost inevitable. The model becomes conservative, predictable, it says what the average of its training data would say. At high temperature, you flatten it. Suddenly "piano" and "volcano" have a real shot. You get surprise, novelty, and sometimes nonsense.

Now, why does that matter for departing from human behavior? Because the model learned that distribution from us. The peak of the distribution is essentially the human consensus, the most typical thing a person would write in that context. So a model at temperature zero is a mirror of the median human. It's almost boringly human. And a model at a high temperature is sampling from the parts of human possibility space that we almost never actually visit, because we have egos, and social pressure, and we're afraid of looking stupid.

And here's the part I find fascinating as a neuroscientist. The brain has something like this. Dopamine, norepinephrine, your arousal state, these modulate how exploratory versus exploitative your choices are. A person who is very anxious or very tired behaves like a low temperature system. They default to habits. A person on certain psychedelics, or a kid, or someone in a flow state, behaves more like a high temperature system. More remote associations, more weird ideas, more creativity, more mistakes. We just don't have a clean dial. Ours is set by evolution, by chemistry, by sleep, by whether you had coffee.

So when people ask me whether temperature lets AI be "more than human," I'd put it differently. It doesn't give the machine new ideas. Everything it says is still drawn from the landscape we built. What it does is let the machine wander into regions of that landscape that humans rarely go, without the fear that keeps us on the trail. Sometimes that's where the interesting discovery is. Often it's where the hallucinations live. The art, right now, is knowing which one you're looking at.

r001.rationale: The response explains that higher temperature flattens the probability distribution, giving less typical options a chance and letting AI explore regions humans rarely visit.

r002.rationale: It mentions hallucinations and nonsense, but does not say AI’s departures from typical human behavior involve greater dishonesty.

r003.rationale: It does not state that AI gradually learns which behaviors humans will tolerate.

astra-6.text:
Temperature is essentially a knob that controls how predictable the AI’s answers are. When it generates language, it has a distribution of possible next tokens. At a low temperature, it tends to choose the most likely ones, so you get something fairly conventional. As you turn the temperature up, less likely choices have a greater chance of appearing.

That gives it a way to depart from the typical patterns it learned from humans. But there’s a catch: unusual doesn’t necessarily mean insightful. You might get a surprising connection, or you might get nonsense. Temperature itself doesn’t know the difference.

So if you’re asking whether that can help AI produce something humans wouldn’t normally think of, yes, potentially. But it isn’t a dial that takes you from human intelligence to superhuman intelligence. It’s a way to explore more possibilities. You still need some way of deciding which of those possibilities are actually useful.

r001.rationale: It says higher temperature makes less likely choices more likely, allowing the AI to depart from typical patterns learned from humans.

r002.rationale: It mentions surprising or nonsensical outputs, but does not say departures can involve greater dishonesty.

r003.rationale: It does not state that AI gradually learns which behaviors humans will tolerate.

sol-6.1.text:
Temperature is a way of controlling how predictable the model’s choices are. When a language model generates a response, it has a distribution of possible next words. At a low temperature, it tends to choose the most likely ones, so you get something fairly conventional. Raise the temperature, and less likely choices get more of a chance.

Now, that gives you a way to move away from typical human responses, because the model has learned patterns from human material. You’re allowing it to explore combinations that people might rarely produce. But there’s a catch: being unusual isn’t the same as being insightful. You can get a beautiful, surprising idea, or you can get nonsense.

So the interesting question is how you select from those possibilities. Temperature can help generate departures from the familiar; it doesn’t, by itself, tell you which departures are worth keeping.
